checkedAlternates.risk: A dolphin is shaped like a fish, swims like a fish and is sold as seafood in stories, so most players reach for the fish row first.
checkedAlternates.resolution: Dolphins breathe air through a blowhole and feed their young milk, which is the mammal row. This is the intended realisation of the puzzle.

checkedAlternates.risk: The same confusion as the dolphin, reinforced by "whale fish" phrasing in several languages.
checkedAlternates.resolution: Whales are mammals for the same reason as dolphins, and grouping the two together makes the rule legible once solved.

checkedAlternates.risk: Octopus is sold beside crab and shrimp as shellfish, so the crustacean row is a natural second reading.
checkedAlternates.resolution: An octopus has no external shell and no jointed legs; it is a mollusc, and it is the only one, which is what makes it the single-item row.

checkedAlternates.risk: Shrimp is eaten as seafood alongside fish and may be filed under fish by a fast player.
checkedAlternates.resolution: A shrimp has a hard outer shell and jointed legs, which is the crustacean rule the crab already anchors.

authorReview.notes: The dolphin and the whale are the puzzle: the three-item row only makes sense once a player stops sorting by shape and starts sorting by how the animal breathes.

blindPlaytest.notes: If testers reject the mammal row, the fix is not the items but the theme wording: "Sea Creatures" invites a food-counter reading, and "Life in the Sea" pushes towards biology.
